en: Bring torment upon the Kazakhs;
Bring ruin upon his people,
And sate yourself at Kök-Muroo.
Saying, “These are the Kazakhs you have seen,”
Bring back many captives roped at the waist.
You were a hero and a lion;
Your words give me joy.
If anyone could strike a warrior, it was you;
Your fame has remained with me.
Ah, Külchoro, my foal,
Say, “These are my uncle’s words,”
And tell them to Ümötöy.
If he brings calamity upon the Kazakhs,
Convey my greetings and blessing!”
So saying, Semetey
Fired and sharpened his companion’s spirit,
Strengthened him, and sent him on his way.
The lion companion flew like an arrow,
The valiant companion like a naked blade,
To the banks of Üch-Koshoy,
And the lowlands of great Keng-Kol.
Külchoro galloped there
And reached the appointed place.
Seeing the companion, Ümötöy
Took his steel spear in hand,
Struck Kulaker once on the flank,
And made him pound hollows into the earth;
With matchless agility,
He sent him racing at full speed,
And came up to the companion.
When valiant Ümötöy approached,
The noble companion made ready like a trained falcon;
The splendid hero’s brave companion
Found wisdom as though from the unseen.
Speaking softly but with firm resolve,
With matchless tact,
Külchoro began to speak
And went before Ümötöy:
“Ümötöy, my cousin through our mothers,
You have come because reedy Keng-Kol and broad Talas
Seemed fine lands to you.
You have come because the precious people
Of the forty Kyrgyz tribes seemed a nation worth having.
You have come because Semetey, son of Manas,
The heroic, fierce-wolf sultan,
Seemed their mainstay.
Do not seethe and work yourself up;
Cast aside your vicious intent,
And form a new purpose.
Offer the sultan wise counsel,
And, whether it brings sin or merit,
Take upon yourself the duty
Of Kazakh and Kyrgyz alike.
As for the aged lion Bakay,
My hero, we mean to grant you
Everything you have requested.
Ümötöy, cousin through our mothers,
If you are sane and not mad,
If you are a warrior and not an enemy,
You have become a fortress before the champions.
If you listen to reason, Ümötöy,
You shall become this year a mighty hero and lord,
Not only among the Kyrgyz but throughout the world.
In the lowlands of Jylgynduu,
On the banks of broad Talas,
In place of the hero Köksö,
You whose tidings are mighty and name renowned,
We intend to make you khan.
Throughout all lands
Seen by eyes and heard of by ears,
We intend to make you khan.
We shall proclaim,
‘Ümötöy has become exalted,’
And make you lord
Over all the prosperous people.
Willingly accept the khanship;
Go before my uncle, the bloodthirsty khan,
And say that you are his kinsman.
Here is a head to take, and here is the land;
Hero, if you would take a head, here am I.
If you receive them well, here are the willing Kyrgyz
And their whole nation!
If you turn violent, here am I,
The noble companion who will take your head!
Put all your resentment aside;
Cease working yourself into a fury.
At heart we are brothers of one blood;
Abide by the words that have been spoken.
Heed what has been said.
Towering like a blue cliff,
My lord, wherever you appear,
Do not quarrel with the lion,
With the heroic, fierce-wolf warrior.
A prince becomes a true prince
Through the multitude of his people.
If you make peace, Ümötöy,
Semetey will say, ‘My cousin, my soul’s companion, has come,’
And, sparing nothing,
Will give you countless dark-maned mares,
And camels numbered in their thousands.”
So saying, Külchoro
Stood before Ümötöy
And delivered these words.
Growing furious and obstinate,
That wretched Ümötöy
Was now struck by God.
His eyes blazed with rage;
Good heavens, his bloodlust seized him fiercely.
Turning sideways and working himself up,
He shouted in madness:
“The fly-like life within my breast,
And my spoonful of black blood,
I shall sacrifice to battle.
Look what this damned, wretched slave
Has dared to do!
Spouting smooth, broad words,
Talking of a time when life will be sweet—
Look at the words uttered
By this fool whose life has fled him!
You two renowned, fierce lions,
Who have girded your belts,
Do not appear, companion,
Before my eyes again!
Become night without first growing dark,
And, miserable slave, bathe not merely in blood—
Become one with your blood!
If I do not meet you in single combat,
If I alone do not destroy
Your army covering the earth,
May I die no longer Ümötöy,
May I sink away as though never born!
Unless he pays the blood-price for my father,
Unless he yields to my grievance,
Unless he loads up six measures of gold
And draws the high-stepping Buurul
Beneath me here and now—
See what words this ill-starred wretch
Has just spoken!
One of you is Khan Semetey,
Who sits there as khan;
Ümötöy’s wrath has risen,
And now he will beat the frenzy from you.
I came demanding my khan-father’s blood-price;
It was for this purpose I came.
Who told you to make anyone khan?
Look at the words uttered
By this wretch who deserves a shameful death!
Look at what this damned companion
Has dared to do!
Tell me of your tawny, rolling hills;
Do not prattle on,
But tell me how you mean to fight.
The matter, in brief, is this:
I will not prosper by befriending Semetey
And riding at his side.
Nor can I accept Külchoro and aged Bakay
Even if they are given to me as slaves.
I shall rage as your neighbor,
Destroy your camp and swallow it whole.
I shall bring doom upon your people,
And slaughter your nation to the last.
I shall raze your ancestral fortress;
If I do not bring utter ruin upon you all,
Then, slave companion who came between us,
May I fail to kill you before I go!
Will I not find a way to master you?
Will I not stain my spear with your blood,
Cut short your years,
And sever your head, you accursed slave?”
So raging, Ümötöy
Took a blue-steel spear
With a steel shaft and sharpened point,
And struck Kulager once.
Fire boiled beyond his eyes,
And he bit hard enough to split his lip.
He shouted torrents of words,
Raising Köksö’s battle cry.
His shout could split a head,
The force of his voice could shatter stone.
Pouring out his fury, he lunged,
Refusing to turn from bloodshed;
He armed himself with his heavy musket,
Prepared himself, crying, “Stand and do not flee!”
He confronted
The noble hero in his wrath.
Ümötöy entered the fray;
Ümötöy entered a tumult
From which no one could find escape.
His brass spear was edged with steel,
Fit for the broad ravine no bay horse could cross,
A spear from which no living soul escaped.
Ümötöy had truly committed himself;
Stiff with fury,
The madman reached his foe.
“The face of the gray coat of mail,” he thought,
“The lower edge of the heart,
The very point I measured,
The fatal spot to strike;
If I thrust a little farther,
That is the heart itself.”
He attacked Külchoro.
The many Kazakhs behind him
Burst forward in a wild charge.
The surpassing wrestler Ümötöy
Made his companion’s armor ring
With a mighty spear thrust.
Külchoro, lion of the wilds,
Did not so much as grunt when the spear struck.
If struck by a battle-axe, the fierce one
Would never budge from his place.
He stood firm and paid it no heed,
Counting Ümötöy’s thrust
As nothing beside his boot-heel.
The Lord Most High had granted the companion
Valor and lionheartedness
Beyond all measure.
His fortune was complete;
That Külchoro was a true warrior.
He took no account of high or low;
Such was his heroism
That he gave no thought to dying.
He turned the mouth of Surkoën,
The broad-rumped, mattock-hoofed steed
He rode into battle.
“How many more tricks have you, hero?
If your own strength is not enough,
Call all your Kazakhs,” he said,
And stood laughing boldly.
Ümötöy of the Kazakhs
Thrust not once but ten times,
Reeling there like a slave.
Though he struck twenty times, Külchoro paid no heed,
Counting it as nothing beside his boot-heel.
The lion Külchoro stood and said:
“By your father’s grave, Ümötöy,
It seems you have no sense at all.
Put aside this frenzy.
Your strength alone cannot prevail;
Bring on your strongest men—
Your excited Kazakhs, your nation of ten thousand.
Fire your heavy muskets and draw your bows;
If you have the strength, slaughter me.
Do not prance about, Kazakh host;
Stop, or you will be scattered.
You came as a guest, yet stand there bristling;
Do not stir up a bitter quarrel.
Do not let every last one of you
Perish in a massacre.
Do not push matters to the bitter end,
Lest your survivors say
That I crushed and overwhelmed the dead.
Become a moonless night;
Ümötöy and your two thousand Kazakhs,
Become one with all your people.
When I thrust with wrath boiling,
Would I prosper if I shrank from you,
